sections.html:
Milford is a shoreline city in New Haven County, squeezed between its two larger neighbors, New Haven and Bridgeport. Its 2020 population was 50,558. Roughly 25 square miles make up the city, with water accounting for more than 3 of them.

The shoreline runs over 14 miles, the longest of any Connecticut town. Much of it is Silver Sands State Park, which includes Charles Island, a protected bird nesting ground. The city also takes in the village of Devon, at the mouth of the Housatonic River, and the borough of Woodmont. With that much waterfront, a buyer's first questions usually concern flood zone status, salt damage and upkeep. Have answers ready.

sections.h2: Beach communities, boroughs and who bills you
sections.html:
Milford is split into named communities, and several face the water. Downtown Milford, Devon and Rivercliff are joined by a run of beach neighborhoods: Walnut Beach, Wildermere Beach, Laurel Beach, Point Beach, Bayview and Morningside.

Six of these are chartered by Special Act of the General Assembly and have some municipal powers, taxing authority among them. Woodmont is a borough with all statutory municipal powers, yet it remains part of the city. So an address in one of these areas may carry a charge on top of the city tax bill.

  • Find out whether your property sits in a borough, a beach association or a chartered community.
  • Ask that body whether it charges taxes or fees of its own.
  • Ask the city which tax collector bills your address.

Residents can use five lifeguarded public beaches: Gulf Beach, Anchor Beach, Hawley Avenue Beach, Walnut Beach and Middle Beach. Seven beaches are private.

sections.h2: Milford property taxes and the Tax Collector
sections.html:
One office, the Tax Collector, sends the real estate, motor vehicle and personal property bills, and the same desk takes sewer use fees, sewer assessments and sewer laterals. Each October 1 the Assessor's Office certifies the Grand List those bills are built on.

The Board of Aldermen sets the mill rate through the adopted city budget, and the Sewer Commission sets the sewer use fee. The city cannot override Connecticut statutes. Land use goes through a separate Planning and Zoning Board.

  • Office: 70 West River Street, First Floor, Room 105.
  • Mailing address: PO Box 3025, Milford, CT 06460-0825.
  • Phone: 203-783-3217, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed on holidays.
  • The office also runs a tax calculator and a mill rate history page.

A call to this office before you pick a closing date saves trouble. Request a balance that covers sewer charges too. Anything still owed generally comes out of your proceeds at the table.

sections.h2: What a Milford seller pays when the deed is recorded
sections.html:
Connecticut puts its conveyance tax on the seller at the moment of recording. The town clerk receives Form OP-236 and holds the deed back until payment is made.

Piece of the taxTypical home saleGoes to
State portion0.75 percent (higher above $800,000)State of Connecticut
Municipal portion0.25 percentCity of Milford

C.G.S. 12-494 is the governing statute. Exemptions exist for a principal residence sold in lieu of foreclosure and for certain defective-foundation sales.

Short sales get their own treatment: when a principal residence brings less than the mortgages plus the priority tax and sewer liens, the state exempts the transfer. Anyone in that spot needs an attorney's read before signing.

Old land records in Milford hold one strange chapter. Starting in 1902, Quaker Oats boxes carried coupons for deeds to tiny lots in a never-built Liberty Park subdivision. The town ended those lots in the mid-1970s through a general foreclosure. It shows why a title search is worth the small fee, since a clean chain of ownership is what lets a deed record without delay.

sections.h2: Getting around: rail, highway and bus
sections.html:
I-95 and U.S. Route 1 run through Milford's southern end. The Wilbur Cross Parkway takes the north. A link road, the Milford Parkway (also called the Daniel S. Wasson Connector), joins that parkway to I-95 and Route 1.

  • The Metro-North New Haven Line stops at a downtown Milford station with direct service to New York City.
  • The Milford Transit District runs in-town service.
  • Connections reach Greater Bridgeport Transit, Norwalk Transit District and CT Transit New Haven.

If a long commute is why you are leaving, you can still describe the convenient address honestly to a buyer.

sections.h2: Who tends to sell in Milford
sections.html:
People selling in Milford include owners of aging beach cottages, families winding up an estate, and landlords with multi-unit buildings. Coastal houses bring upkeep questions that unsettle buyers, and a lender may scrutinize flood zone status.

Going the listing route means repairs, showings and a financing contingency. An as-is cash sale removes all three. Get both numbers and pick the one that suits your calendar.

  • Gather tax bills, sewer bills and any association invoices.
  • Check for beach association or borough charges.
  • Confirm who holds title and whether an estate is involved.

If the house has had water in the basement, a roof patch or a past insurance claim, write down what happened and what was done about it. Buyers and their insurers ask, and a plain account from the owner is easier to trust than a vague answer. A rushed seller often forgets small items, like where the oil tank or the shutoff valves are, so walk the house once with a notepad before anyone else does.

sections.h2: Steps from first call to closing
sections.html:
1. Give the buyer your address, a candid description of the house and your preferred closing date.
  2. A walk-through follows, and then a written offer that you are free to decline.
  3. If you say yes, a title company or attorney opens the file, runs the title search and requests a payoff letter from your mortgage lender.
  4. Unpaid taxes, sewer charges and liens are subtracted from your proceeds.
  5. On closing day you sign the deed, the conveyance tax return goes to the town clerk, and the deed is recorded.

Bring photo ID, your latest mortgage statement, recent tax and sewer bills, and every key and garage opener you have. Since no buyer's lender is involved in a cash sale, there is no loan approval or appraisal to wait on, and the pace is set mostly by the title work. For legal or tax questions, ask a Connecticut attorney or the city office.

It also helps to decide in advance what stays with the house. Appliances, window treatments and anything in the shed or garage should be settled in writing, and anything you plan to take should be cleared out before the final walk-through. Forward your mail and cancel automatic payments tied to the property once the sale is recorded.

faqs.q: How much shoreline does Milford have?
faqs.a: Over 14 miles on Long Island Sound, the most of any Connecticut town. Much of it is Silver Sands State Park.

faqs.q: Do Milford's beach communities tax separately?
faqs.a: Some do. Six chartered communities have taxing authority, and Woodmont is a borough with full municipal powers. Ask whether your address falls inside one.

faqs.q: Where is the Milford Tax Collector?
faqs.a: At 70 West River Street, First Floor, Room 105. Call 203-783-3217, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
The Board of Aldermen sets it through the adopted city budget, working from the Grand List certified each October 1. The Sewer Commission sets sewer use fees.

faqs.q: Who pays the conveyance tax in Milford?
faqs.a: The seller, at recording. A standard home sale is 0.75 percent to the state and 0.25 percent to the city, with a higher state rate above $800,000.
